section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: The food cultivation system of the Native American groups referenced in the stimulus above is most analogous to which of the following North American indigenous food systems?

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

options: (A) Buffalo hunting among the Lakota Sioux
(B) Wolf domestication by the Algonquians
(C) Mixed agriculture among the Iroquois
(D) Seal hunting among the Inuit
items.explanation: The Native groups referenced in the stimulus were sedentary agriculturalists, cultivating crops in permanent settlements. Their food system is most analogous to mixed agriculture among the Iroquois — the three-sisters farming of corn, beans, and squash. Both were settled, crop-based economies, unlike the hunting economies of the Plains or Arctic.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Buffalo hunting was a nomadic Plains economy, not the sedentary farming of the referenced groups.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Wolf domestication was not a food system analogous to crop agriculture.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The referenced groups' farming is most analogous to mixed agriculture among the Iroquois.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Seal hunting was an Arctic subsistence economy, not agriculture.

items.stem: In the decades after 1492, contact between Spaniards and Native Americans produced all of the following EXCEPT The engraving above (c. 1600) depicts Europeans' arrival in the Americas — the contact whose consequences the question tests.

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Discovery of America,' engraving after Stradanus, Nova Reperta series, c. 1600.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Engraving c.1600 after Johannes Stradanus (Nova Reperta series); Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0

options: A. Epidemics that devastated Native communities
B. The rapid adoption of horses and cattle by Native peoples
C. Missionary efforts to convert Native peoples to Catholicism
D. American crops such as maize and potatoes reaching Europe
items.explanation: In the decades immediately after 1492, contact produced devastating epidemics, missionary conversion efforts, and the Columbian Exchange of crops — but not the rapid adoption of horses and cattle by Native peoples. Horses and cattle spread slowly over generations; Native equestrian cultures emerged much later. Rapid adoption belongs to a later era, not the first decades of contact.

option_explanations.A: Contact did produce this, so it is not the answer. Epidemics devastated Native communities from the earliest contact.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Native peoples did not rapidly adopt horses and cattle in the decades after 1492.
option_explanations.C: Contact did produce this, so it is not the answer. Catholic missionaries began converting Natives immediately.
option_explanations.D: Contact did produce this, so it is not the answer. Maize and potatoes reached Europe in the Columbian Exchange.

items.stem: The above excerpts support which one of the following generalizations?

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

options: (A) After European and Latin American populations interacted economically, most Europeans were more compassionate toward the interests of non-white people.
(B) There was some degree of debate by Spanish explorers over how to treat natives in the New World.
(C) The appeal to natural rights and natural law succeeded in abolishing slavery in the New World.
(D) The European belief in white superiority was used to justify the doctrine of natural rights.
items.explanation: Aristotle's defense of natural slavery alongside Glendon's account of Latin American human-rights thought points to the great Spanish debate over the treatment of Native peoples — Las Casas versus Sepúlveda, the Valladolid controversy. The excerpts show that how to treat the natives was genuinely contested, not settled. The generalization is that Spanish explorers and thinkers debated the natives' humanity and rights.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The excerpts show debate, not European compassion toward non-white interests.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The excerpts support that Spanish thinkers debated how to treat natives in the New World.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Natural-law appeals did not abolish New World slavery.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The excerpts do not show white superiority justifying natural-rights doctrine.

items.stem: Why were confrontations such as those in the excerpt rare in the New England colonies? Pyle's 1905 painting above depicts the burning of Jamestown during Bacon's Rebellion (1676).

stimulus.pd_rationale: Howard Pyle, 1905; pre-1930 publication
stimulus.text_stimulus: The Burning of Jamestown, 1676 “Whereas complaint has been made to this Board by Capt. William Pierce, Esq., that six of his servants and a negro of Mr. Reginald’s has plotted to run away unto the Dutch plantation from their said masters,…the court taking the same into consideration as a dangerous precedent for the future time (if left unpunished), did order that Christopher Miller, a Dutchman (a prime agent in the business), should receive the punishment of whipping,…the said Peter Milcocke to receive thirty stripes and to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R,…said Richard Cockson, after his full time Expired with his master, to serve the colony for two years and a half, and the said Richard Hill to remain upon his good behavior until the next offense, and the said Andrew Noxe to receive thirty stripes, and the said John Williams, a Dutchman and a [surgeon] after his full time of service is Expired with his master, to serve the colony for seven years, and Emanuel, the Negro, to receive thirty stripes and to be burnt in the cheek with the letter R and to work in shackles one year or more as his master shall see cause.” Source: General Court Responds to Runaway Servants and Slaves Minutes of the Council and General Court of Colonial Virginia, 1640

options: (A) New England populations were largely homogenous with economies based on subsistence farming, rather than cash crops.
(B) Puritan law forbade the sale or ownership of enslaved people.
(C) Indentured servants in New England were largely treated fairly, serving for short terms before gaining freedom.
(D) Negotiations after King Philip’s War had ensured the return of indentured servants back to Europe.
items.explanation: Bacon's Rebellion erupted in Virginia from the explosive mix of cash-crop tobacco agriculture, land-hungry former servants, and frontier Indian policy. New England lacked that mix: its population was largely homogeneous and its economy based on subsistence farming rather than cash crops, so the rebellion's social tinder never accumulated. Confrontations like Bacon's were rare where the causes were absent.

option_explanations.A: Correct. New England's homogenous population and subsistence economy prevented Bacon-style confrontations.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Puritan law did not forbid slave ownership; New Englanders did own enslaved people.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Indentured servants were not treated so fairly or briefly as to explain the difference.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No such negotiations after King Philip's War returned servants to Europe.

items.stem: What change in the southern colonies' slave system began in the 1730s?
options: A. The Dutch lost their slave-trade monopoly, flooding the colonies with captives
B. Conditions on the Middle Passage grew noticeably milder
C. Enslaved people increasingly lived and worked on large plantations
D. Slave revolts led planters to ease working conditions
items.explanation: Beginning in the 1730s, enslaved people in the southern colonies increasingly lived and worked on large plantations — the consolidation of the plantation system as tobacco and rice operations grew. Small farms and urban slavery gave way to the great gang-labor plantations of the mature South. The 1730s mark the plantation's ascendancy in the slave system.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Dutch lost their trade role a century earlier, not in the 1730s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Middle Passage did not grow milder in the 1730s.
option_explanations.C: Correct. From the 1730s, enslaved people increasingly lived and worked on large plantations.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Slave revolts did not ease working conditions; they hardened them.

options: (A) English colonists sought to control the native populations through missions and religious conversions.
(B) Trade alliances with Native Americans promoted the economic health of early Chesapeake settlements.
(C) A shortage of indentured servants led to the emergence of the African slave trade.
(D) Chesapeake labor-intensive agriculture used both white and African indentured servants
items.explanation: Pyle's painting of Bacon's Rebellion — the burning of Jamestown — supports the conclusion that Chesapeake labor-intensive agriculture used both white and African indentured servants. The rebellion's ranks included poor whites and Black laborers together, united against the colonial elite. The painting testifies to the mixed, exploited labor force of the early Chesapeake.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Missions and conversions were the Spanish pattern, not the Chesapeake's.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Trade alliances with Natives were not Bacon's Rebellion's subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The excerpt concerns indentured labor's unrest, not the slave trade's emergence.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The painting shows Chesapeake agriculture's reliance on both white and African indentured labor.

items.stem: Unlike the French and Spanish colonies, the seventeenth-century English colonies were distinguished by

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James... Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation..."
—Mayflower Compact, 1620 (abridged)

options: A. Home governments that discouraged emigration
B. Large-scale family settlement that displaced Native peoples from the land
C. Populations made up mainly of male fur traders and missionaries
D. Settlement concentrated in a few fortified trading posts
items.explanation: The Mayflower Compact's covenant of self-government was carried to America by whole families who settled in numbers large enough to displace Native peoples from the land. Unlike the French and Spanish colonies — with their fur traders, missionaries, and fortified posts — English America was built by family settlement. Large-scale settlement, not extraction, was the English colonial distinction.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. English home governments encouraged emigration; that was their advantage.
option_explanations.B: Correct. English colonies were distinguished by large-scale family settlement displacing Native peoples.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Male fur traders and missionaries describe French and Spanish colonies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Fortified trading posts were the French and Spanish pattern, not the English.

items.stem: Hamilton's diagnosis in this passage most directly foreshadowed which of the following developments?

stimulus.text: "We may... be said to have reached almost the last stage of national humiliation. There is scarcely any thing that can wound the pride or degrade the character of an independent nation which we do not experience... Do we owe debts to foreigners and to our citizens...? There remains without any proper or satisfactory provision for their discharge. Is commerce of importance to national wealth? Ours is at the lowest point of declension." — Alexander Hamilton, Federalist No. 15, 1787

options: (A) The rise of Democratic-Republican societies opposing the Washington administration.
(B) The addition of a Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties from federal power.
(C) The drafting of a Constitution creating a stronger national government with powers to tax and regulate commerce.
(D) The issuance of Washington's Proclamation of Neutrality in the war between Britain and France.
items.explanation: Hamilton's 1780 diagnosis — national humiliation, unpaid debts, commerce at its lowest point — foreshadowed the drafting of a Constitution creating a stronger national government with powers to tax and regulate commerce. The Articles' impotence, which Hamilton catalogued, was exactly what the Philadelphia Convention was called to cure. His diagnosis became the Constitution's prescription.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Democratic-Republican societies came in the 1790s, not as a direct foreshadowing of Hamilton's diagnosis.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Bill of Rights protected liberties; Hamilton's complaint was about fiscal and commercial weakness.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Hamilton's diagnosis foreshadowed the Constitution's stronger national government with tax and commerce powers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Neutrality Proclamation was 1793 foreign policy, not the answer to Hamilton's fiscal diagnosis.

items.stem: Jefferson's embargo most closely resembles

stimulus.image_caption: 'Ograbme, or the American Snapping-Turtle,' embargo cartoon, 1807.
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 1-4 refer to the cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. The Open Door policy in China
B. The Good Neighbor Policy
C. Manifest Destiny
D. The Neutrality Laws of the 1930s
items.explanation: Jefferson's embargo tried to keep America out of the Napoleonic Wars by cutting off trade — using economic disengagement as a substitute for war. The 1930s Neutrality Laws did the same thing: Congress legislated non-involvement to keep America out of Europe's wars. Both were attempts to buy peace through economic withdrawal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Open Door policy promoted trade access in China, the opposite of an embargo.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Good Neighbor Policy was about Latin American diplomacy, not economic withdrawal.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Manifest Destiny was territorial expansion, not trade restriction.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Jefferson's embargo most closely resembles the Neutrality Laws of the 1930s.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a contributing factor in the crafting of the United States Constitution?

stimulus.text: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816

options: (A) Individual state constitutions written at the time of the Revolution tended to cede too much power to the federal government, leading to a call for reform on the part of Anti-Federalists.
(B) The weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation led James Madison to question their efficacy and prompted a formation of the Constitutional Congress in 1787.
(C) Difficulties over trade and foreign relations led to a repeal of overly restrictive tariffs required by the Articles of Confederation.
(D) Washington’s embarrassing failure at the Whiskey Rebellion led to Federalist demands for a new framework for federal power.
items.explanation: Jefferson's letter — arguing that laws and institutions must advance with the human mind — reflects the framers' willingness to remake government when it failed. The Articles of Confederation's weaknesses led Madison to question their efficacy and prompted the Constitutional Convention of 1787. The Constitution was crafted because the Articles had failed.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. State constitutions did not cede too much power to the federal government; the Articles gave it too little.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Articles' weaknesses prompted Madison and the 1787 Constitutional Convention.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Tariffs were not repealed under the Articles; Congress lacked tariff power entirely.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Whiskey Rebellion came in 1794, after the Constitution was ratified.

items.stem: Which was a reference to slavery in the Constitution?

stimulus.image_caption: 'To be sold, on board the ship Bance-Island... negroes,' slave-sale broadside, Charleston, 1760 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Printed 1760 broadside; Library of Congress (item 98503865), pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 5-8 refer to the broadside above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. The Northwest Ordinance's slavery ban
B. Slavery outlawed above the Mason-Dixon Line
C. Slavery could never be outlawed
D. No federal ban on slave importation for 20 years
items.explanation: The Constitution referenced slavery without naming it — most notably in the provision barring any federal ban on slave importation for twenty years. The framers compromised: the trade could continue until 1808, and then Congress could prohibit it. Slavery was in the Constitution from the start, protected by deliberate euphemism.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Northwest Ordinance was a separate 1787 law, not part of the Constitution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Constitution drew no Mason-Dixon ban on slavery.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Constitution did not declare slavery could never be outlawed.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Constitution barred a federal ban on slave importation for 20 years.

items.stem: All of the following features of the Constitution were designed to mitigate the problems described by Washington in the excerpt EXCEPT

stimulus.text: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796

options: (A) the popular election of representatives to the House
(B) the indirect election of senators by state legislatures
(C) the use of an electoral college to select a president
(D) the nomination of judges to the Supreme Court by the executive branch
items.explanation: Washington warned against the spirit of party, and the framers designed filters against popular faction: senators chosen by legislatures, presidents by the Electoral College, judges nominated by the executive. The popular election of House representatives was not such a filter — it was the one direct democratic channel, the people's house. It did not mitigate party spirit; it expressed it.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Popular House election did not mitigate the party spirit Washington feared.
option_explanations.B: This was designed to mitigate it, so it is not the answer. Indirect senatorial election filtered popular passions.
option_explanations.C: This was designed to mitigate it, so it is not the answer. The Electoral College was a deliberative filter.
option_explanations.D: This was designed to mitigate it, so it is not the answer. Executive nomination insulated judges from faction.

items.stem: After the Revolution, many Founders believed

stimulus.image_caption: 'To be sold, on board the ship Bance-Island... negroes,' slave-sale broadside, Charleston, 1760 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Printed 1760 broadside; Library of Congress (item 98503865), pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 5-8 refer to the broadside above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. Slavery would gradually disappear
B. Freeing slaves should be outlawed
C. Slavery would anchor the economy
D. Freed slaves deserved reparations
items.explanation: After the Revolution, many Founders — Jefferson and Madison among them — believed slavery would gradually disappear: the Revolution's ideals, they thought, would make it wither. They were wrong. The cotton gin and westward expansion made slavery more profitable than ever. But the expectation of gradual extinction was genuinely held in the 1780s.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Many Founders believed slavery would gradually disappear.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. No Founder proposed outlawing emancipation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Founders did not celebrate slavery as the economy's anchor; many expected its decline.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Reparations were not proposed by the Founders.

items.stem: Jefferson and Hamilton disagreed on all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. How powerful the federal government should be
B. American tariff policy
C. The need for a national bank
D. Whether the Constitution was the supreme law
items.explanation: Jefferson and Hamilton disagreed about federal power's size, about tariffs, and about the national bank — the great debates of the 1790s. But both accepted the Constitution as the supreme law of the land; their quarrel was over what it meant, not whether it bound them. Constitutional supremacy was common ground, not contested territory.

option_explanations.A: They did disagree on this, so it is not the answer. Federal power's extent was their central quarrel.
option_explanations.B: They did disagree on this, so it is not the answer. Tariff policy divided them.
option_explanations.C: They did disagree on this, so it is not the answer. The bank was their famous fight.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Both accepted the Constitution as supreme law.

items.stem: Thomas Jefferson relied on the ideas of John Locke in writing the American Declaration of Independence in all of the following ways EXCEPT Locke’s belief that
options: (A) man is born free and equal
(B) man must submit to the General Will
(C) governments get their authority from the people, not God
(D) the purpose of government is to protect man’s natural rights
items.explanation: Jefferson drew from Locke the ideas that men are born free and equal, that governments derive authority from the people, and that government's purpose is protecting natural rights. But the General Will — the idea that man must submit to it — is Rousseau's, not Locke's. Jefferson's Declaration is Lockean, not Rousseauian.

option_explanations.A: Jefferson did use this, so it is not the answer. Born free and equal is Locke's and the Declaration's.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The General Will is Rousseau's idea, not Locke's.
option_explanations.C: Jefferson did use this, so it is not the answer. Popular authority over divine right is Lockean.
option_explanations.D: Jefferson did use this, so it is not the answer. Protecting natural rights is Locke's core idea.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in the excerpt most directly challenged the prevailing ideal in the 19th century that

stimulus.text: “Neither here, nor in any other part of the world, is the right of suffrage allowed to extend beyond one of the sexes. This universal exclusion of woman…argues, conclusively, that, not as yet, is there one nation so far emerged from barbarism, and so far practically Christian, as to permit woman to rise up to the one level of the human family.” Source: U.S. Representative Gerrit Smith, 1848

options: (A) women should enjoy full and equal rights with men
(B) women’s political interests were sufficiently represented by their husbands and fathers
(C) the presence of women in industry and agriculture was a positive step toward independence
(D) women were responsible for the education of their children
items.explanation: Gerrit Smith's 1848 speech — denouncing woman's universal exclusion from suffrage as barbarism — most directly challenged the prevailing nineteenth-century ideal that women's political interests were sufficiently represented by their husbands and fathers. The doctrine of virtual representation held that women needed no vote because men voted for them; Smith called that a sham. His target was representation-by-proxy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Full equal rights for women was Smith's position, not the ideal he challenged.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Smith challenged the ideal that husbands and fathers sufficiently represented women's interests.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Women's presence in industry was not the prevailing ideal Smith attacked.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Maternal responsibility for children's education was not the ideal under challenge.

items.stem: The cartoon most directly reflects opposition to

Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[An 1832 anti-Jackson cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson in royal robes and a crown, clutching a veto message in one hand while trampling the Constitution and the Bank of the United States underfoot.]

options: A. The Tariff of Abominations and the nullification controversy
B. The Indian Removal Act and the forced migration of the Cherokees
C. The spoils system and rotation of federal officeholders

option_explanations.B: Wrong. Indian removal was not the cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The spoils system was a separate Jacksonian issue.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The cartoon reflects opposition to Jackson's executive power claims, especially the Bank veto.

items.stem: The nature of both Adams’ and Polk’s excerpts above best reflect which of the following common views of the 19th century?

stimulus.text: Source 1: “The whole continent of North America appears to be destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation, speaking one language, professing one general system of religious and political principles, and accustomed to one general tenor of social usages and customs. For the common happiness of them all, for their peace and prosperity, I believe it is indispensable that they should be associated in one federal Union.” Source: John Quincy Adams, letter to his father, 1811 Source 2: “In assuming responsibilities so vast I fervently invoke the aid of that Almighty Ruler of the Universe in whose hands are the destinies of nations and of men to guard this Heaven-favored land against the mischiefs which without His guidance might arise from an unwise public policy. With a firm reliance upon the wisdom of Omnipotence to sustain and direct me in the path of duty which I am appointed to pursue, I stand in the presence of this assembled multitude of my countrymen to take upon myself the solemn obligation ‘to the best of my ability to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States.” Source: James Polk, Inauguration Speech, 1845

options: (A) Laissez-faire economics
(B) Social Darwinism
(C) Manifest Destiny
(D) Nativism
items.explanation: Adams's vision of one nation peopling the continent and Polk's expansionism both express Manifest Destiny — the nineteenth-century belief that America was divinely destined to spread across North America. Divine Providence peopling the continent is the doctrine's purest statement. Both excerpts are Manifest Destiny in different voices.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Laissez-faire economics is not the excerpts' theme.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Social Darwinism came later, after Darwin.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Both excerpts reflect the common nineteenth-century view of Manifest Destiny.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Nativism targeted immigrants, not continental expansion.

items.stem: Which group would have most strongly supported the act's perspective?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1848 (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) Participants in the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848.
(B) Southern defenders of the traditional Southern ideal of 'female virtue.'
(C) Champions of the 'cult of domesticity.'
(D) Congregational ministers.
items.explanation: The act — presumably a women's rights measure — would have been most strongly supported by participants in the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848: the organized women's rights movement's founding gathering. Seneca Falls demanded legal equality for women, and its participants were the natural constituency for any such act. Southern traditionalists, domesticity champions, and Congregational ministers generally opposed it.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Seneca Falls participants would most strongly support the act's perspective.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southern defenders of female virtue opposed women's legal equality.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Cult-of-domesticity champions confined women to the home.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Congregational ministers were not the act's natural supporters.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed by Jackson above would have been most shared with which of the following?

stimulus.text: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? Their power would be great whenever they might choose to exert it; but if this monopoly were regularly renewed every fifteen or twenty years on terms proposed by themselves, they might seldom in peace put forth their strength to influence elections or control the affairs of the nation. But if any private citizen or public functionary should interpose to curtail its powers or prevent a renewal of its privileges, it cannot be doubted that he would be made to feel its influence.” Source: President Andrew Jackson, Veto of the Bank of the United States, 1832

options: (A) An oil magnate at the turn of the 20th century
(B) A supply-side economist in the 1980s
(C) A Federalist elected official in the 1790s
(D) A midwestern farmer in the 1890s
items.explanation: Jackson's Bank veto message — denouncing a self-elected directory serving foreign stockholders — spoke the language of producerist populism against financial monopoly. A midwestern farmer in the 1890s would have shared it completely: Populists and their heirs hated banks, railroads, and eastern money power with Jacksonian fervor. The sentiment bridges 1832 and 1892.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. An oil magnate embodied the monopoly power Jackson attacked.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A supply-side economist would defend the financial order Jackson denounced.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. A 1790s Federalist favored the bank; Jackson's heirs opposed it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. A midwestern 1890s farmer would most share Jackson's anti-bank sentiment.

items.stem: The 1848 Married Women's Property Act is best understood in the context of which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1848 (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus: "The real property of any female who may hereafter marry... shall not be subject to the sole disposal of her husband, nor be liable for his debts, and shall continue her sole and separate property, as if she were a single female.... Any married female may take by inheritance, or by gift... and convey and devise real and personal property... in the same manner and with like effect as if she were unmarried." — Married Women's Property Act, New York, 1848

options: (A) The Know-Nothing movement against immigration.
(B) The temperance crusade against alcohol.
(C) The abolition of slavery in New York.
(D) The emerging women's rights movement, which held the Seneca Falls Convention in the same year.
items.explanation: The 1848 Married Women's Property Act — letting married women own property in their own names — belongs to the context of the emerging women's rights movement, which held the Seneca Falls Convention in the same year. Property rights were the movement's first legal victory; the convention's Declaration of Sentiments demanded them. The act and the convention are the same year's twin milestones.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Know-Nothing movement targeted immigrants, not women's property.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Temperance fought alcohol, not coverture.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. New York slavery's abolition was 1827, two decades earlier.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The act belongs to the emerging women's rights movement of 1848.

items.stem: Jackson's policy most directly produced which outcome?
options: (A) Lasting peace between Native tribes and white settlers
(B) The forced removal of the Cherokee from their southeastern homeland
(C) The first Treaty of Fort Laramie, securing western lands for the tribes
(D) A negotiated settlement permitting the southeastern tribes to remain on their lands for another decade
items.explanation: Jackson's Indian removal policy most directly produced the forced removal of the Cherokee from their southeastern homeland — the Trail of Tears. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorized the expulsions; the Cherokee's forced march west was its most infamous result. Removal, not peace or negotiation, was the policy's product.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Jackson's policy produced war and removal, not lasting peace.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Jackson's policy most directly produced the forced Cherokee removal.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Fort Laramie treaty concerned Plains tribes, not Jackson's southeastern removals.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No negotiated decade-long reprieve resulted; removal was forced.

items.stem: Which twentieth-century development continued the attitudes Thomas describes?
options: (A) The Great Migration
(B) Jim Crow legislation
(C) The Civil Rights Act of 1957
(D) The 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
items.explanation: Thomas's attitudes — presumably white-supremacist views of Black inferiority — were continued into the twentieth century by Jim Crow legislation: the segregation laws that encoded racial hierarchy after Reconstruction's end. Disenfranchisement, separate cars, and separate schools were the legal heirs of the attitudes Thomas expressed. Jim Crow carried them forward.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Great Migration was Black Southerners' response to oppression, not its continuation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Jim Crow legislation continued the attitudes Thomas describes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Civil Rights Act of 1957 opposed those attitudes, not continued them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The 1963 March challenged the attitudes, not continued them.

items.stem: Which of the following was a major Northern military advantage during the Civil War?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1861 (J. B. Elliott; entered per Act of Congress; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)

options: A. Fighting on familiar home territory
B. A unified public opinion behind the war
C. Far greater industrial output and railroad networks
D. A long tradition of cavalry service
items.explanation: The North's decisive military advantage was material: far greater industrial output and railroad networks. Northern factories produced the rifles, rails, and ships; Northern railroads moved armies and supplies at a scale the South could not match. Industry and railroads were the Union's arsenal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Familiar home territory was the Confederacy's advantage, not the North's.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Northern public opinion was divided; Copperheads opposed the war.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The North's major advantage was far greater industrial output and railroad networks.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The South, not the North, had the cavalry tradition.

items.stem: American settlers first entered Mexican Texas in the early 1830s
options: A. To avenge the Alamo
B. From disillusionment with U.S. Indian policy
C. Out of loyalty to Crockett or Bowie
D. Because Mexico offered vast tracts nearly free
items.explanation: American settlers first entered Mexican Texas in the early 1830s because Mexico offered vast tracts nearly free: empresario grants gave colonists enormous holdings for almost nothing. Cheap land, not revenge or loyalty, drew them. The Alamo came later; the land came first.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Alamo was 1836; settlers arrived before it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Disillusionment with Indian policy did not draw settlers to Texas.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Crockett and Bowie were not the settlers' motive.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Settlers came because Mexico offered vast tracts nearly free.

items.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the Emancipation Proclamation?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published September 22, 1862 (preliminary proclamation). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) It guaranteed the freedom of every enslaved person within the boundaries of the United States once the Civil War concluded.
(B) It freed enslaved people only in states and parts of states then in rebellion.
(C) It made emancipation conditional on southern states signing a peace treaty.
(D) It barred enslaved people from serving as soldiers in either army.
items.explanation: The Emancipation Proclamation was a war measure, not a universal abolition: it freed enslaved people only in states and parts of states then in rebellion — precisely where Lincoln's authority as commander-in-chief reached. It freed no one in the loyal border states and no one in Union-occupied territory. Its limits were constitutional, not accidental.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Proclamation did not guarantee freedom to every enslaved person; it was limited to rebel areas.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Proclamation freed enslaved people only in areas then in rebellion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Emancipation was not conditional on a peace treaty.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Proclamation authorized Black military service; it did not bar it.

items.stem: Lincoln's position in the passage differs from that of radical abolitionists chiefly in which of the following ways?

stimulus.text: "It is the sentiment around which all their [Republicans'] actions, all their arguments, circle, from which all their propositions radiate. They look upon it as being a moral, social, and political wrong; and while they contemplate it as such, they nevertheless have due regard for its actual existence among us.... Yet... they desire a policy in regard to it that looks to its not creating any more danger. They insist that it should, as far as may be, be treated as a wrong; and one of the methods of treating it as a wrong is to make provision that it shall grow no larger." — Abraham Lincoln, debate with Stephen Douglas, October 1858

options: (A) It calls for the forced colonization of freed Black people outside the United States.
(B) It endorses popular sovereignty as the proper way to settle slavery in the territories.
(C) It demands immediate, uncompensated emancipation of all enslaved people.
(D) It accepts slavery's existing legal presence while insisting slavery be treated as a moral wrong and prevented from expanding.
items.explanation: Lincoln's 1850s position accepted slavery's existing legal presence — he would not touch it where it stood — while insisting slavery be treated as a moral wrong and prevented from expanding into the territories. Radical abolitionists demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation everywhere; Lincoln offered containment with moral condemnation. The difference was strategy and scope, not sympathy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Forced colonization was a separate Lincoln idea, not the chief difference from abolitionists.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lincoln opposed popular sovereignty on slavery; he did not endorse it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Immediate uncompensated emancipation was the abolitionists' demand, not Lincoln's.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Lincoln accepted slavery's legal presence while treating it as a moral wrong to be contained.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why South Carolina chose to secede from the Union in 1860?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Original diagram generated by the committed fixed-seed script gen_election_maps.py (this directory). No third-party source; electoral data cross-checked against published state-by-state results.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860

options: (A) The failures of the Compromise of 1850 hindered South Carolina’s trade relationships with Western states, leading to severe economic recession.
(B) The Battle of Fort Sumter occurred in Charleston, prompting public outrage over Union aggression.
(C) President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation, thus undermining slavery in the South.
(D) Lincoln’s election on a Free-Soil platform led southern politicians to conclude that secession was necessary.
items.explanation: South Carolina seceded in December 1860 because Lincoln's election on a Free-Soil platform convinced southern politicians that the federal government would now work against slavery's interests. A Republican president meant no more slavery expansion — and, they feared, eventual abolition. Secession was their preemptive answer to Lincoln's victory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Compromise of 1850's failures did not cause South Carolina's secession.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Fort Sumter came after secession, not before it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Emancipation Proclamation was 1863, two years after secession.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Lincoln's Free-Soil election led South Carolina to secede.

items.stem: Anthony's activism contributed most directly to the ratification of
options: (A) The Nineteenth Amendment
(B) The Equal Rights Amendment
(C) The Fifteenth Amendment
(D) The Twenty-sixth Amendment
items.explanation: Susan B. Anthony's lifelong activism for women's suffrage contributed most directly to the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment (1920), which finally granted women the vote. The amendment was even called the Anthony Amendment in her honor. Her cause became the Constitution's nineteenth article.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Anthony's activism contributed most directly to the Nineteenth Amendment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Equal Rights Amendment was never ratified.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Fifteenth Amendment enfranchised Black men, not women.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Twenty-sixth Amendment lowered the voting age to eighteen.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would be most likely to support the perspective of Frederick Douglass?
options: (A) Southern Democrats in the 1880s
(B) Western ranchers in the 1850s
(C) Southern farmers in the 1830s
(D) Northern Republicans in the 1860s
items.explanation: Frederick Douglass's perspective — abolition, Black citizenship, equal rights — would have been most likely supported by Northern Republicans in the 1860s: the party of Lincoln that passed the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments. Douglass advised Republican presidents and campaigned for their cause. The party and the prophet were allies.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Southern Democrats in the 1880s built Jim Crow; they opposed Douglass's perspective.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Western ranchers in the 1850s were not Douglass's constituency.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Southern farmers in the 1830s defended slavery.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Northern Republicans in the 1860s would most support Douglass's perspective.

items.stem: Which of the following failed to strengthen the legality of the Sherman Antitrust Act?

stimulus.text: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890

options: (A) Passage of the Clayton Antitrust Act
(B) Passage of the Interstate Commerce Act
(C) Formation of the Federal Trade Commission
(D) Implementation of the McKinley Tariff
items.explanation: The Clayton Antitrust Act, the Interstate Commerce Act, and the Federal Trade Commission all strengthened antitrust enforcement — closing loopholes and adding machinery. The McKinley Tariff did none of that: it raised protective tariffs, a trade policy unrelated to competition law. Tariffs and trusts were separate battles.

option_explanations.A: This strengthened the Sherman Act, so it is not the answer. Clayton closed antitrust loopholes.
option_explanations.B: This strengthened the Sherman Act, so it is not the answer. The ICC added regulatory machinery.
option_explanations.C: This strengthened the Sherman Act, so it is not the answer. The FTC enforced competition law.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The McKinley Tariff did nothing to strengthen the Sherman Antitrust Act.

items.stem: Which best expresses Nast's perspective in this cartoon?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Harper's Weekly, 1871-10-21 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A Thomas Nast cartoon depicting Tammany Hall boss William M. Tweed as a bloated, grasping figure looming over New York City.]

options: A. Tammany's leadership benefits New York
B. New Jersey exploits New York City
C. The federal government oppresses the city
D. Boss Tweed wields too much power
items.explanation: Thomas Nast's cartoons — his Tammany Hall series — express the perspective that Boss Tweed wields too much power: the bloated boss looming over New York, devouring public money. Nast was Tweed's great journalistic nemesis, and his drawings made the boss's corruption visible. The cartoon is an indictment of Tweed's power.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Nast did not believe Tammany benefited New York; he believed it robbed the city.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. New Jersey's exploitation was not Nast's subject.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Federal oppression was not the cartoon's theme.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Nast's perspective is that Boss Tweed wields too much power.

items.stem: The Dawes Act
options: A. Sought to turn Native Americans into individual farmers
B. Shielded Native land from further white encroachment
C. Split large reservations into smaller ones
D. Outlawed the Ghost Dance
items.explanation: The Dawes Act of 1887 sought to turn Native Americans into individual farmers: it broke up tribal lands into individual allotments, aiming to dissolve tribal life and assimilate Indians as Jeffersonian yeomen. The surplus went to white settlers; the tribes lost most of their land. Assimilation through the plow was the act's design — and its disaster.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Dawes Act sought to turn Native Americans into individual farmers.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Dawes Act accelerated land loss; it did not shield Native land.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The act allotted individual parcels; it did not split reservations into smaller ones.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Ghost Dance was suppressed by military force, not outlawed by Dawes.

items.stem: The “new immigrants” who arrived in the United States after the Civil War were different from the “old immigrants” in that they

stimulus.pd_rationale: Puck, 1880 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.

options: (A) came mostly from Latin American countries
(B) settled in rural areas in the Midwest where land was plentiful
(C) were better prepared than previous immigrants had been to face the challenges of urban life
(D) came from southern and eastern Europe, speaking unfamiliar languages
items.explanation: The new immigrants who arrived after the Civil War — Italians, Poles, Russians, Jews — came from southern and eastern Europe, speaking unfamiliar languages and practicing unfamiliar religions. The old immigrants had come from northern and western Europe. The new immigration's origins defined the era's nativist backlash.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Latin American immigration grew later, in the twentieth century.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. New immigrants settled in cities, not rural Midwestern farms.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. New immigrants were less prepared for urban life, not better.
option_explanations.D: Correct. New immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe with unfamiliar languages.

items.stem: Which best explains the price trend shown in the table?
options: (A) the growth of family farms in the 1870s and 1880s as thousands of 'new immigrant' families settled the rural Midwest.
(B) Population stagnation from birth control and a growing middle class
(C) Agricultural mechanization and expanded acreage creating surpluses
(D) Latin American surpluses flooding U.S. markets
items.explanation: The wholesale farm-price index's long decline from 140 (1866) to 56 (1896) is best explained by agricultural mechanization and expanded acreage creating surpluses: steel plows, reapers, and railroads opened vast new lands, and production outran demand. More crops meant lower prices. Overproduction, not immigration or Latin competition, broke farm prices.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Family-farm growth was a result of expansion, not the price trend's cause.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Population stagnation is not the explanation; overproduction is.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Mechanization and expanded acreage created the surpluses behind falling prices.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Latin American surpluses did not flood U.S. markets in this era.

items.stem: Efforts to curb corporate power in the 1890s and 1900s were most significantly limited by which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Puck, 1889-01-23 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) Congress passed antitrust laws but presidents routinely vetoed them.
(B) Reformers, politicians, and labor leaders quickly succeeded in restructuring the economy.
(C) Most Americans rejected antitrust efforts as communistic and un-American.
(D) Supreme Court rulings narrowed antitrust law, shielding manufacturers from regulation.
items.explanation: Efforts to curb corporate power in the 1890s and 1900s were most significantly limited by Supreme Court rulings that narrowed antitrust law, shielding manufacturers from regulation — E.C. Knight (1895) gutted the Sherman Act by ruling manufacturing was not interstate commerce. The Court, not Congress or public opinion, was the great obstacle. Reform ran aground on judicial interpretation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Presidents did not routinely veto antitrust laws; Congress passed them.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Reformers did not quickly succeed; the economy was not restructured.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Most Americans did not reject antitrust as communistic.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Supreme Court rulings narrowed antitrust law and shielded manufacturers.

items.stem: All of the following states were admitted to the union in the post-war 19th century EXCEPT
options: (A) North Dakota
(B) Wyoming
(C) Arizona
(D) Washington
items.explanation: North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Washington, Idaho, and Wyoming were all admitted in 1889–1890, the post-war nineteenth century's great statehood wave. Arizona was not: it became a state in 1912, well into the twentieth century. Arizona is the exception.

option_explanations.A: North Dakota was admitted in 1889, so it is not the answer.
option_explanations.B: Wyoming was admitted in 1890, so it is not the answer.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Arizona was admitted in 1912, not in the nineteenth century.
option_explanations.D: Washington was admitted in 1889, so it is not the answer.

items.stem: Truman issued this press release primarily to

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

President Truman's August 1945 announcement told the nation that an American plane had dropped a single bomb on Hiroshima with explosive force equal to more than 20,000 tons of TNT — a weapon, he said, that would shorten the agony of war.
—After President Harry Truman's press release, August 6, 1945

options: A. to declare war on Japan
B. to announce and justify the use of a revolutionary new weapon
C. to announce Japan's surrender
D. to secretly warn the Soviet Union
items.explanation: Truman issued the August 6, 1945 press release primarily to announce and justify the use of a revolutionary new weapon: the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. The release told the nation what had happened, described the bomb's unprecedented power, and framed it as shortening the war's agony. It was announcement as justification — the bomb explained and defended.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The United States was already at war with Japan; no declaration was needed.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Truman's release announced and justified the revolutionary new weapon.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Japan had not surrendered; the surrender came days later.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The release was public, not a secret warning to the Soviets.

items.stem: Parker's review of McPherson's autobiography is best described as

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1913 photograph (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

options: A. A witty demolition of celebrity self-promotion
B. An earnest endorsement of McPherson's ministry
C. A theological defense of religious fundamentalism
D. A neutral summary of the book's plot
items.explanation: Parker's review of Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography is best described as a witty demolition of celebrity self-promotion: a sharp, amused takedown of the evangelist's self-mythologizing. Parker punctured the celebrity preacher's inflated self-portrait with her famous irony. The review is demolition disguised as book criticism.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Parker's review was a witty demolition of celebrity self-promotion.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Parker did not earnestly endorse McPherson's ministry.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The review was not a theological defense of fundamentalism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Parker was anything but neutral; her review was pointed satire.

items.stem: What best accounts for the sharp increase of immigrants during the period 1880–1910?

stimulus.text: “Since the foundations of the American commonwealth were laid in colonial times over 300 years ago, vigorous complaint and more or less bitter persecution have been aimed at newcomers to our shores. Also the congressional reports of about 1840 are full of abuse of English, Scotch, Welsh immigrants as paupers, criminals, and so forth. Old citizens in Detroit of Irish and German descent have told me of the fierce tirades and propaganda directed against the great waves of Irish and Germans who came over from 1840 on for a few decades to escape civil, racial, and religious persecution in their native lands. The “Know-Nothings,” lineal ancestors of the Ku-Klux Klan, bitterly denounced the Irish and Germans as mongrels, scum, foreigners, and a menace to our institutions, much as other great branches of the Caucasian race of glorious history and antecedents are berated to-day…. But to-day it is the Italians, Spanish, Poles, Jews, Greeks, Russians, Balkanians, and so forth, who are the racial lepers…. In this bill we find racial discrimination at its worst—a deliberate attempt to go back 84 years in our census taken every 10 years so that a blow may be aimed at peoples of eastern and southern Europe, particularly at our recent allies in the Great War—Poland and Italy.” Source: Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record , 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924

options: (A) Many Southern and Eastern Europeans turned to America for financial gain and political freedom.
(B) Irish farmers were forced to leave their homes because of agricultural disasters.
(C) Germans were seeking ways to avoid military conscription.
(D) The United States welcomed immigrants by providing housing and employment.
items.explanation: The sharp increase in immigration during 1880–1910 came because many Southern and Eastern Europeans turned to America for financial gain and political freedom: Italians, Poles, Jews, and others fled poverty, persecution, and conscription for American wages and liberty. Push factors at home and pull factors in America drove the new immigration. The era's immigrants sought bread and freedom.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Southern and Eastern Europeans came for financial gain and political freedom.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Irish flight from agricultural disaster was the 1840s, not 1880–1910.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Avoiding German conscription was a minor factor, not the main driver.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The United States did not provide housing and employment to immigrants.

items.stem: Riis's purpose in detailing the woman's wages and meals was to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by Jacob Riis, 1888 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)

options: A. Praise the woman's thrift and industry
B. Shock comfortable readers into demanding reform
C. Recruit workers for the factory
D. Defend tenement landlords
items.explanation: Riis detailed the woman's wages and meals — her pennies, her scraps — to shock comfortable readers into demanding reform. The point of the precise, pitiful numbers was moral indictment: no reader could see what she lived on and defend the system. Riis's statistics were weapons aimed at the conscience.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Riis did not praise her thrift; he indicted the system that starved her.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Riis's purpose was to shock comfortable readers into demanding reform.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Riis was not recruiting factory workers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Riis attacked tenement landlords; he did not defend them.

items.stem: One group of women who kept their jobs through the Depression was
options: A. Schoolteachers
B. Clerical workers
C. Domestic workers
D. Government employees
items.explanation: Domestic workers — maids, cooks, and household servants — were one group of women who kept their jobs through the Depression. Middle-class families still needed household help, and domestic work could not be mechanized or postponed. While factories and offices shed women workers, the demand for household labor persisted.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Schoolteachers faced layoffs and marriage bars during the Depression.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Clerical workers were laid off as businesses contracted.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Domestic workers kept their jobs through the Depression.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Government employment was limited; the New Deal's jobs programs came later.

items.stem: A reader sympathetic to the cartoon would most likely also have supported which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by Jacob Riis, 1888 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: (A) The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.
(B) The Spanish-American War of 1898.
(C) The Supreme Court's Insular Cases decisions on overseas territories.
(D) The settlement-house movement serving the urban poor.
items.explanation: The cartoon — presumably a Progressive-era image of urban suffering or immigrant sympathy — would appeal to a reader who also supported the settlement-house movement serving the urban poor. Both express the same humane impulse: go to the slums, live among the poor, and relieve their suffering. The cartoon and Hull House are the same reform instinct in different media.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Chinese Exclusion Act persecuted immigrants; it contradicts the cartoon's sympathy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Spanish-American War was imperialism, unrelated to the cartoon's reform sympathy.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Insular Cases upheld colonial rule; they do not match the cartoon's spirit.

items.stem: The immediate issue behind Beveridge's speech was whether to

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)

options: A. Purchase Alaska
B. Invade Canada
C. Annex the Philippines
D. Join the League of Nations
items.explanation: Beveridge's March of the Flag — the march of the flag farther westward and southward — was delivered in September 1898, when the immediate issue was whether to annex the Philippines, the prize of the Spanish-American War. Beveridge answered yes: empire was America's destiny. The speech was the annexation debate's great manifesto.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Alaska was purchased in 1867, three decades earlier.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Invading Canada was never the issue.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The immediate issue behind Beveridge's speech was annexing the Philippines.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The League of Nations was 1919, two decades later.

items.stem: The stock market crash of 1929 was the result of which of the following? Irresponsible lending by banks and corporations Overspeculation of the value of the stock market Failure of banks to guarantee the security of deposits
options: (A) II only
(B) I and II only
(C) II and III only
(D) I, II, and III
items.explanation: The 1929 crash resulted from all three: irresponsible lending by banks and corporations, overspeculation that inflated stock values beyond reality, and banks' failure to guarantee deposit security. Easy credit fed the bubble; the bubble's burst destroyed unprotected deposits. The crash was a three-part failure of the financial system.

option_explanations.A: Incomplete, so it is not the answer. Overspeculation alone does not capture the full causes.
option_explanations.B: Incomplete, so it is not the answer. It omits the banks' failure to secure deposits.
option_explanations.C: Incomplete, so it is not the answer. It omits irresponsible lending.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The crash resulted from I, II, and III together.

President Reagan argued that raising taxes would not shrink deficits: revenues had risen sharply in 1980, he claimed, yet the deficit still hit record highs — proof, in his view, that the problem was runaway spending, not insufficient taxes.

items.stem: King wrote the 'Letter from a Birmingham Jail' most directly in response to which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-USIA}}: U.S. Information Agency photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus: In his 1963 'Letter from a Birmingham Jail,' Martin Luther King Jr. defended his presence in Birmingham, arguing that injustice anywhere threatens justice everywhere and that all communities are bound in a single 'network of mutuality.' He rejected the charge that he was an 'outside agitator': anyone living in the United States, he wrote, can never be considered an outsider anywhere in the country. (Paraphrased from 'Letter from a Birmingham Jail,' April 16, 1963.)

options: (A) His election to the United States Congress.
(B) The passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
(C) A public statement by white clergymen urging Black citizens to withdraw support from the demonstrations.
(D) The Supreme Court's verdict in the Montgomery bus boycott case.
items.explanation: King wrote the Letter from a Birmingham Jail in April 1963 most directly in response to a public statement by eight white Alabama clergymen urging Black citizens to withdraw support from the demonstrations — calling the protests unwise and untimely. King's letter answered their criticism point by point, defending direct action. The clergymen's statement was the letter's occasion.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. King was never elected to Congress.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 came a year after the letter.
option_explanations.C: Correct. King responded to the white clergymen's statement urging withdrawal from demonstrations.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Montgomery bus boycott verdict was 1956, seven years earlier.

items.stem: Spock's advice differed from earlier child-rearing experts in urging parents to

stimulus.text:

Dr. Benjamin Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) reassured parents that child-rearing was a natural process: trust your instincts, the book counseled, for 'you know more than you think you do' — a permissive message that resonated with a generation raising children in unprecedented prosperity.

options: A. Trust their natural instincts rather than rigid schedules
B. Follow strict feeding and sleeping schedules
C. Send young children to boarding schools
D. Avoid physical affection with their babies

option_explanations.B: Wrong. Strict schedules were the old experts' advice that Spock rejected.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Boarding schools were not Spock's recommendation.

items.stem: Supply-side economics held that wealthy tax-cut recipients would do all of the following EXCEPT

options: A. Invest heavily in the economy
B. Open new factories
C. Buy stocks

It did not hold that they would dramatically increase their savings: hoarding was the opposite of the promised productive investment. Savings, not enterprise, was the exception.

option_explanations.A: Supply-siders expected this, so it is not the answer. Investment was the theory's core promise.
option_explanations.B: Supply-siders expected this, so it is not the answer. New factories were the promised result.
option_explanations.C: Supply-siders expected this, so it is not the answer. Stock purchases counted as investment.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Supply-side theory did not promise dramatically increased savings.

items.stem: Reagan's distinction between powers granted to the federal government and those 'reserved to the states or the people' invokes which of the following?

stimulus.text: In his 1981 inaugural address, President Ronald Reagan declared that 'government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem,' pledged to curb the size and influence of the federal establishment, and insisted on the distinction between powers granted to the federal government and those reserved to the states or the people — reminding listeners that the states created the federal government, not the reverse. (Paraphrased.)

options: (A) The Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause.
(B) The Commerce Clause.
(C) The First Amendment's establishment clause.
(D) The Tenth Amendment.
items.explanation: Reagan's distinction between federal powers and those reserved to the states or the people invokes the Tenth Amendment: powers not delegated to the United States are reserved to the states or the people. The amendment is the Constitution's federalism clause, and Reagan's inaugural made it a governing philosophy. The Tenth Amendment was his text.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause is not the reserved-powers doctrine.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Commerce Clause expands federal power; it does not reserve state power.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The establishment clause concerns religion, not federalism.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Reagan's distinction invokes the Tenth Amendment.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historians argue that few laws reshaped modern America as unexpectedly as the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965. Meant as a modest civil-rights correction to the discriminatory national-origins quotas of the 1920s, the act instead transformed the nation's demographics: by prioritizing family reunification and opening immigration beyond Europe, it brought millions of newcomers from Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. By 2000, nearly one in ten Americans was foreign-born, and cities from Los Angeles to New York were profoundly reshaped. The new immigration enriched American culture and the economy - but it also ignited fierce debates over assimilation, bilingualism, and the meaning of American identity.
questions.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about immigration after 1965.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific law or policy changed immigration after 1965.
C. Briefly explain ONE political controversy caused by the immigration changes described in the passage.
exemplar: The passage argues that the 1965 Immigration Act transformed America more profoundly than its authors intended: by ending discriminatory quotas, it made the United States a far more diverse nation, especially through immigration from Asia and Latin America.
The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quota system and prioritized family reunification, opening legal immigration to regions long excluded.

The new diversity sparked nativist backlash: critics argued immigrants strained social services and changed American culture, fueling debates over bilingual education, border enforcement, and - by the 2000s - comprehensive immigration reform.

questions.stimulus_text: They are well built, with good bodies and handsome features... They do not bear arms, and do not know them, for I showed them a sword, they took it by the edge and cut themselves out of ignorance. They would make fine servants.
questions.attribution: Christopher Columbus, journal entry, October 12, 1492 (abstract by Bartolome de las Casas).
parts: A. Briefly describe Columbus's impression of the Native peoples he met, as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE aspect of Taino culture that shaped this first encounter.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of Spanish colonization for the Taino within fifty years of this encounter.
exemplar: Columbus describes the Taino as physically impressive, generous, and technologically simple - people who had never seen steel weapons and did not understand their danger.
The Taino practiced gift-giving and communal sharing, which Columbus misread as childlike simplicity rather than a different cultural system of exchange and obligation.

Within decades the Taino population of Hispaniola collapsed - from disease, overwork in Spanish mines under the encomienda system, and violence - one of the first demographic catastrophes of the Columbian Exchange.

questions.stimulus_text: The following bar graph compares Union and Confederate military deaths during the Civil War, 1861–1865: approximately 360,000 Union dead and 260,000 Confederate dead, with disease listed as the largest single cause of death in both armies, ahead of battle wounds.
parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE conclusion supported by the data in the graph.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the scale of wartime death affected American society after 1865.
C. Briefly explain ONE limitation of the graph for evaluating Rhodes's argument about Northern and Southern attitudes.
